spans.note: states research hypothesis and describes dataset/scope

spans.assertion: the study used data from 146,028 player-referee dyads from four European leagues, 2012-2013 season
the analysis was designed as exploratory and in-sample to characterize the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis, not confirmatory

after adjusting for games played, physical characteristics, position, and league, dark-skin-toned players had a 0.176 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card (95% CI 0.047-0.302, p=0.008)
this risk difference represents a 16% relative increase over baseline risk
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.159 (95% CI 1.040-1.291, p=0.008), meaning dark-skin-toned players had 15.9% higher odds of a red card
the analysis concludes the hypothesis is supported because the adjusted risk difference is statistically significant and substantively meaningful for a rare outcome
results were robust across multiple sensitivity analyses
the primary point estimate for the adjusted risk difference is 0.176 percentage points
the 95% confidence interval for the risk difference is [0.047, 0.302] percentage points
the two-sided p-value is 0.008 against alpha=0.05
the method used was G-computation (standardization) with parametric bootstrap of 500 iterations

holding covariates constant, dark-skin-toned players (skin tone >= 0.25) have a 0.176 pp higher absolute probability of receiving at least one red card than light-skin-toned players (skin tone < 0.25)
given a baseline risk of ~1.1% in the light-skin group, the effect represents approximately a 16% relative increase
the odds ratio point estimate is 1.159
the 95% confidence interval for the odds ratio is [1.040, 1.291]
the two-sided p-value for the odds ratio is 0.008 against alpha=0.05
dark-skin-toned players have 15.9% higher odds of a red card compared to light-skin-toned players after covariate adjustment

spans.note: section and subsection heading: model/estimation, unit of analysis

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis is player-referee dyads, with n=123,868 after exclusions
the total dyads analyzed is 123,868
there are 1,585 unique players out of 2,053 total in the analysis
there are 3,147 unique referees in the analysis
there are 1,562 red card events (1.26% of dyads)
the light skin group (<0.25) has 51,331 dyads (41.4%) with 568 red card events (1.11%)
the dark skin group (>=0.25) has 72,537 dyads (58.6%) with 994 red card events (1.37%)
dark skin tone was defined as the average of two independent raters' skin tone ratings being >=0.25 on a 0-1 scale
light skin tone was defined as an average rating below 0.25
the 0.25 threshold was chosen because it corresponds to the median of the skin tone distribution and the boundary between very light/light and darker categories on the original 5-point scale
this definition is defensible as a standard epidemiological median-split approach and maximizes sample balance while creating a meaningful contrast

spans.note: description of the original 5-point skin tone scale categories, not a choice made by the analysis

spans.assertion: the outcome was defined as a binary indicator of any red card (1+) received by a player from a referee across all games in the dyad, versus zero
number of games in the player-referee dyad was included as a continuous covariate controlling for exposure time
player height (cm) was included as a continuous covariate
player weight (kg) was included as a continuous covariate
player position was included as a categorical covariate with 5 categories (Defender as reference, Forward, Goalkeeper, Midfielder, Unknown)
league country was included as a categorical covariate with 4 categories (England as reference, France, Germany, Spain)

spans.note: blank / subheading: rationale for covariate selection

spans.assertion: games was included as a covariate because more games means more opportunities for red cards
height and weight were included because they may correlate with playing style, position, and skin tone (anthropometric variation)
position was included because defenders receive more red cards (19.8 per 1000 dyads) than forwards (10.5 per 1000), likely due to defensive responsibilities
league was included because red card rates vary substantially by league (France 16.5 per 1000, Germany 8.8 per 1000), reflecting different disciplinary cultures and referee standards

yellow cards were deliberately excluded from the primary model because they may be mediators (part of the causal pathway) rather than confounders, and including them would underestimate the total effect
a sensitivity analysis including yellow cards showed essentially unchanged results (OR=1.159, p=0.007)
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for missing skin tone ratings (no player photo available or unratable)
this exclusion is justified because the primary exposure cannot be measured without a skin tone rating
photos were unavailable for 467 of 2,053 players in the dataset
753 dyads (0.6% of those with skin tone) were excluded for missing height (n=46) or weight (n=753)
this exclusion follows standard complete-case analysis practice for regression modeling
the impact of this exclusion is minimal, retaining 99.4% of dyads with skin tone data
the total analysis sample is 123,868 dyads, 84.8% of the original 146,028
a logistic regression model was fitted
G-computation (standardization) was used to estimate the adjusted risk difference on the probability scale
standard errors were computed via parametric bootstrap with 500 iterations, sampling coefficients from the asymptotic multivariate normal distribution
inference used a two-sided Wald test for coefficients and the percentile method for the risk difference CI

spans.note: blank / rhetorical subheading: why this approach
general statement about logistic regression properties, not a specific choice justification

spans.assertion: G-computation was chosen because it provides interpretable absolute risk differences on the probability scale, addressing the primary estimand directly
parametric bootstrap was chosen to account for uncertainty in the full covariate-adjusted risk difference
no train-test split or cross-validation was used, consistent with the exploratory goal of characterizing maximal in-sample support
all sensitivity analyses support the primary conclusion and results are robust to alternative skin tone definitions and model specifications

spans.note: blank / subsection heading / table header for alternative thresholds

spans.assertion: the primary threshold (>=0.25) with N dark=72,537 yielded adjusted OR 1.159, adjusted RD 0.176pp, p=0.008
the conservative threshold (>=0.375) with N dark=34,257 yielded adjusted OR 1.131, adjusted RD 0.153pp, p=0.036
the liberal threshold (>=0.125) with N dark=90,361 yielded adjusted OR 1.105, adjusted RD 0.119pp, p=0.102
the primary threshold (>=0.25) yields the strongest and most statistically significant effect among thresholds tested
both more conservative and more liberal threshold definitions show positive effects, with varying precision, and the median-split approach balances sample size, effect size, and statistical power

spans.note: blank / subsection heading: sensitivity analysis 2, yellow cards

spans.assertion: with yellow cards included, adjusted OR is 1.159 [95% CI 1.041,1.292], p=0.007
with yellow cards included, adjusted RD is 0.177pp
results are virtually identical when yellow cards are included, suggesting the skin tone effect is not explained by prior disciplinary history differences
this supports the interpretation that the effect is not purely due to aggressive play style differences

spans.note: blank / subsection heading: sensitivity analysis 3, continuous skin tone

spans.assertion: treating skin tone continuously, the OR per 1-unit increase is 1.274 [95% CI 1.063,1.527], p=0.009
the adjusted risk difference comparing darkest vs lightest is 0.309pp
treating skin tone as continuous reveals a monotonic dose-response relationship where each increment in darkness is associated with higher red card probability
comparing the extremes, the risk difference of 0.31pp is consistent with and slightly larger than the binary comparison

spans.note: blank / subsection heading: effect heterogeneity by league / table header

spans.assertion: in Germany, adjusted OR was 1.444, p=0.002, N=39,433
in Spain, adjusted OR was 1.174, p=0.103, N=31,015
in England, adjusted OR was 1.111, p=0.309, N=34,627
in France, adjusted OR was 0.967, p=0.810, N=18,793
the effect is strongest and most significant in Germany, moderate in Spain and England, and null in France
this heterogeneity may reflect different refereeing cultures, implicit bias levels, or player composition by league

section heading: discussion / subsection heading: evidence strength

spans.assertion: the adjusted risk difference provides directionally consistent and substantively meaningful evidence that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skin-toned players
the two-sided p=0.008 survives the alpha=0.01 threshold
the entire 95% confidence interval lies above zero (0.047 to 0.302pp)
a 16% relative increase over baseline (1.11% to 1.37%) is non-trivial for a consequential outcome since red cards result in ejection and suspension
findings persist across alternative skin tone thresholds, continuous specification, and with/without yellow card adjustment
continuous skin tone shows a monotonic dose-response association (OR per unit=1.27, p=0.009)

spans.note: blank / subsection heading: context and interpretation

spans.assertion: red cards are rare (~1.3% of dyads), so absolute differences are small in percentage points but meaningful in relative terms
a 0.18pp increase on a 1.1% baseline is a 16% relative increase

over a career of ~100 referee dyads, the effect could translate to 18 more red card events per 100 players (110 to 128 per 10,000 dyad-seasons), or roughly 1 additional red card per ~5-6 dark-skin-toned players over their career
given the consequences of red cards, this is a tangible impact

spans.note: comparison to prior research on implicit bias in sports officiating (NBA foul calls, MLB umpire strike zones) and claim the effect size is comparable

spans.assertion: the hypothesis is supported by the data
after adjustment, dark-skin-toned players had a 0.176pp higher probability of a red card (95% CI 0.047-0.302, p=0.008) and adjusted OR of 1.159 (95% CI 1.040-1.291)
